DISCRIMINATIVELY: With discrimination or distinction. J. Foster.
DISENGAGING: Loosing; setting free; detaching. Disengaging machinery. See under Engaging.
DOWERED: Furnished with, or as with, dower or a marriage portion. Shak.
DISPOSURE: 1. The act of disposing; power to dispose of; disposal; direction. Give up My estate to his disposure. Massinger. 2. Disposition; arrangement; position; posture. [Obs.] In a kind of warlike disposure. Sir H. Wotton.
DARIC: 1. (Antiq.) (a) A gold coin of ancient Persia, weighing usually a little more than 128 grains, and bearing on one side of the figure of an archer. (b) A silver coin of about 86 grains, having the figure of an archer, and hence, in modern times, called a daric. 2. Any very pure gold coin.

DOTER: 1. One who dotes; a man whose understanding is enfeebled by age; a dotard. Burton. 2. One excessively fond, or weak in love. Shak.
DISSLANDER: To slander. [Obs.] Legend of Dido. Slander. [Obs.] E. Hall.

DYNAMICALLY: In accordance with the principles of dynamics or moving forces. J. Peile.
DIAPOPHYSIS: The dorsal transverse, or tubercular, process of a vertebra. See Vertebra.
DUMOUS: 1. Abounding with bushes and briers. 2. (Bot.) Having a compact, bushy form.
DECA-: A prefix, from Gr. de`ka, signifying ten; specifically (Metric System), a prefix signifying the weight or measure that is ten times the principal unit.
DISFORESTATION: The act of clearing land of forests. Daniel.
DEPHLEGMATION: The operation of separating water from spirits and acids, by evaporation or repeated distillation; -- called also concentration, especially when acids are the subject of it. [Obs.]
DEAFENING: The act or process of rendering impervious to sound, as a floor or wall; also, the material with which the spaces are filled in this process; pugging.
DRAGONET: 1. A little dragon. Spenser. 2. (Zoöl.) A small British marine fish (Callionymuslyra); -- called also yellow sculpin, fox, and gowdie.

DIPHTHONGAL: Relating or belonging to a diphthong; having the nature of a diphthong. -- Diph*thon"gal*ly, adv.
DULCIFY: 1. (Pharm.) To sweeten; to free from acidity, saltness, or acrimony. Wiseman. 2. Fig. : To mollify; to sweeten; to please. As she . . . was further dulcified by her pipe of tobacco. Hawthorne.
DILIGENT: 1. Prosecuted with careful attention and effort; careful; painstaking; not careless or negligent. The judges shall make diligent inquisition. Deut. xix. 18. 2. DIAPHANOUS: Allowing light to pass through, as porcelain; translucent or transparent; pellucid; clear. Another cloud in the region of them, light enough to be fantastic and diaphanous. Landor.
DABBER: That with which one dabs; hence, a pad or other device used by printers, engravers, etc., as for dabbing type or engraved plates with ink.
DRUIDIC: Pertaining to, or resembling, the Druids. Druidical circles. See under Circle.
DYSURIC: Pertaining to, or afflicted with, dysury.
DETORT: To turn form the original or plain meaning; to pervert; to wrest. Hammond.
DISCORDANCY: State or quality of being discordant; disagreement; inconsistency. There will arise a thousand discordances of opinion. I. Taylor.
DEPARTMENT: 1. Act of departing; departure. [Obs.] Sudden departments from one extreme to another. Wotton. 2. A part, portion, or subdivision. 3. DIPLOMA: A letter or writing, usually under seal, conferring some privilege, honor, or power; a document bearing record of a degree conferred by a literary society or educational institution.
DIFFUSIBILITY: The quality of being diffusible; capability of being poured or spread out.
DECRETAL: Appertaining to a decree; containing a decree; as, a decretal epistle. Ayliffe. 1. (R. C. Ch.) DISTRIBUTABLE: Capable of being distributed. Sir W. Jones.

DURATIVE: Continuing; not completed; implying duration. Its durative tense, which expresses the thought of it as going on. J. Byrne.
DISENTHRALL: To release from thralldom or slavery; to give freedom to; to disinthrall. [Written also disenthral.] Milton.
DUNG: The excrement of an animal. Bacon. 1. To manure with dung. Dryden. 2. (Calico Print.) To immerse or steep, as calico, in a bath of hot water containing cow dung; -- done to remove the superfluous mordant. To void excrement. Swift.
DEPOSITION: 1. The act of depositing or deposing; the act of laying down or thrown down; precipitation. The deposition of rough sand and rolled pebbles. H. Miller. 2. DIGITALIN: (a) (Med.) Any one of several extracts of foxglove (Digitalis), as the "French extract," the "German extract," etc., which differ among themselves in composition and properties. (b) (Chem.) A supposedly distinct vegetable principle as the essential ingredient of the extracts. It is a white, crystalline substance, and is regarded as a glucoside.
DECURRENCE: The act of running down; a lapse. [R.] Gauden.
DIPYRE: A mineral of the scapolite group; -- so called from the double effect of fire upon it, in fusing it, and rendering it phosphorescent.
DISCOUNT: 1. To deduct from an account, debt, charge, and the like; to make an abatement of; as, merchants sometimes discount five or six per cent for prompt payment of bills. 2. DEIST: One who believes in the existence of a God, but denies revealed religion; a freethinker. Note: A deist, as denying a revelation, is opposed to a Christian; as, opposed to the denier of a God, whether atheist or patheist, a deist is generally denominated theist. Latham. Syn. -- See Infidel.
DECIMALIZE: To reduce to a decimal system; as, to decimalize the currency. -- Dec`i*mal*i*za"tion, n.
DENSIMETER: An instrument for ascertaining the specific gravity or density of a substance.
DISSETTLEMENT: The act of unsettling, or the state of being unsettled. Marvell.
DRAWROD: A rod which unites the drawgear at opposite ends of the car, and bears the pull required to draw the train.
DETERGE: To cleanse; to purge away, as foul or offending matter from the body, or from an ulcer.
DOCIBLE: Easily taught or managed; teachable. Milton.
DOS--DOS: Back to back; as, to sit dos-à-dos in a dogcart; to dance dos- à-dos, or so that two dancers move forward and pass back to back. A sofa, open carriage, or the like, so constructed that the occupants sit back to back.
DEKA-: A prefix signifying ten. See Deca-.
DOMETT: A kind of baize of which the ward is cotton and the weft woolen. Blakely.
DELINQUENT: Failing in duty; offending by neglect of duty. One who fails or neglects to perform his duty; an offender or transgressor; one who commits a fault or a crime; a culprit. A delinquent ought to be cited in the place or jurisdiction where the delinquency was committed. Ayliffe.
DREGGINESS: Fullness of dregs or lees; foulness; feculence.
DIBRANCHIATE: Having two gills. -- n. One of the Dibranchiata.
DIMISSORY: Sending away; dismissing to another jurisdiction; granting leave to depart. Letters dimissory (Eccl.), letters given by a bishop dismissing a person who is removing into another diocese, and recommending him for reception there. Hook.
DUCKBILL: See Duck mole, under Duck, n.
DRAGLINK: (a) A link connecting the cranks of two shafts. (b) A drawbar.

DIGNIFIED: Marked with dignity; stately; as, a dignified judge.
DEHISCE: To gape; to open by dehiscence.

DREAR: Dismal; gloomy with solitude. "A drear and dying sound." Milton. Sadness; dismalness. [Obs.] Spenser.

DOBBER: 1. (Zoöl.) See Dabchick. 2. A float to a fishing line. [Local, U. S.]

DRESSY: Showy in dress; attentive to dress. A dressy flaunting maidservant. T. Hook. A neat, dressy gentleman in black. W. Irving.
DULCINEA: A mistress; a sweetheart. I must ever have some Dulcinea in my head. Sterne.
DIZZARD: A blockhead. [Obs.] [Written also dizard, and disard.] -- Diz"zard*ly, adv. [Obs.]
DISPENDER: One who dispends or expends; a steward. [Obs.] Wyclif (1 Cor. iv. 1).
DECORTICATOR: A machine for decorticating wood, hulling grain, etc.; also, an instrument for removing surplus bark or moss from fruit trees.

DEUTEROPATHY: A sympathetic affection of any part of the body, as headache from an overloaded stomach.
DOMINA: Lady; a lady; -- a title formerly given to noble ladies who held a barony in their own right. Burrill.

DEPARTMENTAL: Pertaining to a department or division. Burke.
DISCRADLE: To take from a cradle. [R.] This airy apparition first discradled From Tournay into Portugal. Ford.
DIANDROUS: Of or pertaining to the class Diandria; having two stamens.

DISEMPLOY: To throw out of employment. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.
DESIGNABLE: Capable of being designated or distinctly marked out; distinguishable. Boyle.

DOUCEUR: 1. Gentleness and sweetness of manner; agreeableness. Chesterfield. 2. A gift for service done or to be done; an honorarium; a present; sometimes, a bribe. Burke.

DOXY: A loose wench; a disreputable sweetheart. Shak.

DIURNATION: 1. Continuance during the day. [Obs.] 2. (Zoöl.) The condition of sleeping or becoming dormant by day, as is the case of the bats.

DISCUBITORY: Leaning; fitted for a reclining posture. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

DELICIOUSNESS: 1. The quality of being delicious; as, the deliciousness of a repast. 2. Luxury. "To drive away all superfluity and deliciousness." Sir T. North.
DEARE: variant of Dere, v. t. & n. [Obs.]
DOUBLE-FACED: 1. Having two faces designed for use; as, a double-faced hammer. 2. Deceitful; hypocritical; treacherous. Milton.
DUBITABLE: Liable to be doubted; uncertain. [R.] Dr. H. More. -- Du"bi*ta*bly, adv. [R.]

To destroy or mar the face or external appearance of; to disfigure; to injure, spoil, or mar, by effacing or obliterating important features or portions of; as, to deface a monument; to deface an edifice; to deface writing; to deface a note, deed, or bond; to deface a record. DOUCE: 1. Sweet; pleasant. [Obs.] 2. Sober; prudent; sedate; modest. [Scot.] And this is a douce, honest man. Sir W. Scott.
